name: Acceleration (Overview)
description: Change in velocity—how fast something speeds up, slows down, or changes direction

content.overview: Okay, quick question: have you ever floored the gas pedal and felt yourself pushed back into the seat? That feeling is acceleration. It's really just one question: is your velocity changing? Speeding up, slowing down, even just turning the steering wheel while cruising at a steady speed—all of that counts as acceleration. It's simply ANY change in velocity, whether that's how fast you're going or which way you're headed.
content.explanation:
Here's the whole idea in one line: acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time.

And because velocity is a vector, acceleration is one too—it has a size AND a direction. That's worth remembering.

**Three everyday ways acceleration shows up:**

1. **Speeding up:** You press the gas, the car surges forward. That's acceleration pointing in your direction of travel.
2. **Slowing down:** You hit the brakes. Acceleration is now pointing backward, opposite to your motion (people often call this deceleration, but it's just acceleration with a minus sign).
3. **Changing direction:** Here's the one that trips people up—if you're driving around a curve at a perfectly steady 60 km/h, are you accelerating? Yes! Your speed hasn't changed, but your direction has, and that's still a change in velocity.

**Let's do the math with a real example:**
- Say a car goes from 0 to 60 m/s in 10 seconds (that's seriously fast, but bear with us).
- Acceleration = (60 - 0) m/s ÷ 10 s = 6 m/s²
- In plain English: every second, this car's speed climbs by another 6 m/s.

**The mistake almost everyone makes at first:**
We tend to assume acceleration only means "getting faster." It doesn't! A car braking is accelerating (it's slowing down). A car smoothly turning a corner at constant speed is accelerating (its direction is changing). Any change in velocity—speed, direction, or both—is acceleration. Period.

**Average vs. instantaneous—what's the difference?**
- Average acceleration looks at the big picture: (final velocity − initial velocity) ÷ total time.
- Instantaneous acceleration is what's happening right this second, at one exact moment.

And yes, acceleration can be negative—that just means velocity is decreasing, or the object has reversed direction.

**Units, so you're not caught off guard:**
- We measure acceleration in m/s² (meters per second, per second). Weird-looking unit, we know!
- Don't worry if it feels a little abstract right now—it'll click once you start plugging it into the motion equations coming up next.
keyPoints: Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time (that's it, that's the whole formula)
It's a vector—direction matters just as much as the number
Speeding up, slowing down, or just changing direction: all three count as acceleration
It can absolutely be negative—don't let that throw you
Forces are what cause acceleration in the first place (Newton's laws are coming up next, and this is exactly what sets them up)
content.whyItMatters: Here's why this one matters so much: acceleration is literally what forces produce. Once you're comfortable with it, you've built the bridge from kinematics (just describing motion) to dynamics (explaining why things move the way they do). Basically, everything interesting in mechanics from here on out builds on this idea.
